1.transcript: Transcript: When the Danholt Trough array came up after three years, the record held a surprise. For several weeks in each of those years, the deep current turned around and ran the other way — a reversal, most of a month each time. Season made no difference: winter and summer flows were much the same strength, and the final year ran fully as strong as the first. And this was no quiet current with occasional hiccups; the disturbances ran on for weeks, and between them the flow wandered constantly in strength. Now, the fishing crews' logbooks — one narrow reason: our pressure sensor died with a corrupted timestamp, and a skipper's note about our listing surface buoy dated the failure to the day. That is all they did. The site was chosen off a bathymetric chart years earlier, the catch totals are far too noisy to check anything against, and nothing in the logbooks hints the crews ever noticed the reversals. What next? The old moorings come up for good this autumn — not for another round of the same. A permanent cabled station replaces them, on exactly the same spot, and we will pair its bottom record with a ship survey every spring along the same line. The full series stays in-house for now. Finally, nutrients. I do think this current feeds the shelf: the water arrives still rich, and the rivers here are far too small to account for what we see. But my reason is the plankton — counts bloom within days of each arrival. The sediment traps fill on their own schedule, indifferent to the flow.

5.transcript: Transcript: A logging road opened along the Vireno ridge five years ago, and we have followed the macaque groups through it. Start with the sleeping cliffs. We expected desertion. Instead, all four cliffs stayed in use — including the one nearest the roadbed — and the groups kept their old rotation among them, no cliff more crowded than before. Not once in five years was a group found bedding in the canopy. What changed was the clock: groups that settled at dusk now come in well after dark. My colleague Deren reads this as predator response — leopards moving along the new corridor. I think he has it backwards. The wariness he treats as the driver is itself a product of the disturbance — jumpy animals look predator-pressed. The model's pedigree is not the issue — it was built on forest species in forest much like this — but the evidence for it is thinner than for either rival account, and it never fit even our first season's data. A caution about the follow records. Two teams shadowed two groups in parallel, so same-day comparisons exist. Both seasons fell in the same fruiting year, and every ear notch stayed legible to the end. The real limit is habituation: the boldest groups tolerated observers within weeks; the shyest never quite did, and are thin in the record accordingly. The forestry department acted on the report: within a month, crews were setting out rows of quick-growing figs along the bare roadcut. The road stays open at all hours, no second survey was ordered, and nobody has proposed reserve status for the ridge.

9.transcript: Transcript: Marthe Dole's notebooks, and what the canal company's toll ledgers add. One entry matters most: a payment to M. Dole, for computing the cuttings — she was paid to calculate, not merely to carry a chain, and that is the whole of my point with the ledgers. They record no purchases of instruments, they place her on the western line — the very stretch where the notebooks later surfaced — and the company archive survives virtually complete; the fire of 1774 never reached the ledger room. Dating the pages was harder. The watermarks tell us nothing — that paper stock was in production for fifty years. The ink is uniform from the first page to the last: one sustained campaign of writing, not several. And the notebooks mention no bridge, no lock, no datable structure at all. What settled it was the binding: nineteenth-century work, far younger than the pages, and once it was set aside, the exposed sewing pattern matched an atelier active only in the 1730s. Now, Odile's objection — that Dole's shortcut fails on steep ground. I accept it. The notebooks flag their own hill pages as doubtful, in Dole's hand. The two hill surveys that survive miss badly against modern measurement, contemporaries used the rival tables on steep ground and got it right, and commissions of the period did hire the shortcut for upland work — the failure is real. After her death, the notebooks went to a schoolmaster at Aubrec, who taught from them for thirty years. They were never separated, their whereabouts are documented in every decade since, and Dole left no heirs.

13.transcript: Transcript: The Ansel banner. The fiber and dye analysis gave one discovery: the reds are two different dyestuffs — madder in the original field, a later synthetic in the restitched panels. A repair campaign, then, generations after the weaving. Both reds are true dyes carried in the thread; nothing was brushed onto the finished cloth. The madder is the local strain, from dye-works in the banner's own district, and the colorants show no drift from purple — this red was always red. Why dwell on the 1968 treatment? Not because it haunts us: the backing came away cleanly in 1994 and took the adhesive with it. Not for its photographs, which show the border exactly as the cloth shows it today. And its paperwork never once mentions the discoloration. I describe it because it won a prize — admired, published, imitated — and no conservator alive would defend it now. That is how fast this field moves. The trial cleaning of one corner, next. The stains came away evenly, but the water betrayed us — a tide line crept in as the corner dried, and only a second pass chased it out. Fibers from under the grime tested no different from the exposed areas, and the cleaned corner drapes as softly as the rest. Last, the parish question. There is nothing to debate: the 1961 loan agreement lets the parish recall the banner at will, and preference does not come into it. The church, climate-controlled for years, stays dry the year round; the parish has promised nothing about display; and my lab was never consulted in the dispute.

17.transcript: Transcript: The Sella valley, and Ovel's cylinders. The winter singing evenings first: their real work was survival. By the nineties emigration had emptied farm after farm, and the evenings kept the ballads sung once the households that carried them were gone. No invention of Ovel's day, either — parish complaints about the gatherings run back to the 1740s. Nor did they blend anything together: each farm's version stayed its own — Ovel could tell a Brenholt text from a Vasse by the third line. And print never got in — she found not one broadside in the whole valley. Second, the quarrel over putting the cylinders online. One fact recasts it: the singers' own descendants petitioned for the release, three families in writing. You cannot settle it from Ovel's contracts, which say nothing about publication either way; the archive consulted far beyond the collector's estate; and the wax is in excellent condition, so the cylinders' state is no part of the argument. Third, notebooks beside wax — the striking thing is absence: dozens of songs entered in her hand were never recorded at all; wax was dear, and she rationed it. Where both survive, they match word for word; her texts carry every refrain the wax carries; and every singer she lists is a distinct voice on the cylinders. Last, the customs post at the valley mouth — a boundary and nothing else: past it the Sella ballads stop and the coastal stock takes over. Its ledgers record goods, not travelers; its officers never sang for her; and both her visits are dated to the day in her own diary.

options.B: They took up printed song sheets as readily as the older ballads
options.C: They kept the ballads alive after emigration had emptied the villages

21.transcript: Transcript: The Miren ridge transect, laid out in 1911 by the surveyor Elde, has just been walked again. His photographs first — their value is easy to misstate. Every iron corner marker was found still standing, so relocation needed no pictures; he shot in early July, high season; and his party kept to the trail — the plates show the ledges untrodden. What they uniquely hold is snow: the late snowbeds, photographed year after year, which his written notes never mention — a baseline nothing else provides. The stone daisy: on the ledges it sits where Elde mapped it, but the scree between them is empty — vanished from the loose rock — and no seedlings at all out on the scree. The plants are no larger than his specimens and flower as freely as ever, while the upper limit sits two hundred meters higher, a climb that outran every regional model. The agency report pinned everything on warming. On the crest, I think that is right. But the valley losses track the drainage channels cut in the 1970s, so the report cannot stand as a whole. Grazing is a dead end — sheep never went above the mid-slope fence — and Elde's records are complete for every plot in every year. As for the future: the grant was renewed for a full decade, Elde left no instruction about intervals, and we mean to be back within five years. The worry is the proposed cable-car corridor, cutting straight across the upper plots, possibly before anyone stands here again — and the park has declined to fold the transect into its monitoring.

25.transcript: Transcript: Brenwick's water mains began bursting in the winter of 1871; the inquiry that followed is our subject. Its tests told a simple story: every failed pipe came from a single casting run — the foundry's autumn pour, brittle across all samples — while pipe from other runs in the same streets never failed. The trenches sat in natural gravel that had never been disturbed; the new engines were metered, and pressure never rose past the old maximum; and the bursts came in August as often as in January — so much for frost. Notice, though, the inquiry's stamina: chartered for six months, it sat for five years, long after the public anger had died away — that persistence is the real lesson. Its yard tests were matched deliberately to buried conditions; not one gauge of its own went into the ground — the panel worked from testimony; and the laborers were examined as suspects. Why the rival company across the river? Rates. A decade of undercutting had poisoned everything, and the city would not fund repairs whose cost would surface in that rate war — that is why the money stalled. No one from the rival sat on the panel, the rival never bid for the works — the city itself absorbed them in the end — and the report went to the printers on schedule. The recommendations? Hamburg and Turin wrote them into practice within five years; at home they were never written into any code of the period, not even for the new districts, and when steel mains arrived the testing rules carried over unchanged.

29.transcript: Transcript: Madariaga spent three years inside the Solana wholesale market, and the study still shapes how we think about informal order. His conclusion on the prized corner positions: seniority. Years on the floor decided who moved up when a pitch fell vacant — an order everyone could recite and nobody had written down. Not kinship: sons ranked behind longer-tenured newcomers, and the best pitches did not run in families. Not chance: he hunted for a lottery and found the traders laughing at the idea. Not hidden favors either: the fee books enter every transfer, dated, each matching the seniority queue exactly. Now, the months behind a stall of his own. Readers long puzzled over the silence in his field notes; the explanation is homely — minding the stall left no hand free to write, and the gap is exactly those months. The committee never admitted him; the account before and after keeps its cool distance perfectly; and the pre-dawn auctions he never saw — his stock came by consignment at midday. Bahn's objection, that the traveling vendors are missing, I concede: the census sheets stop at the permanent stalls. And Bahn's list was compiled in the study's final year. But the matters at issue were the fixed positions, where the travelers held no claim, and the omission leaves the central claim standing. The move to the new hall in 1954 is the coda: within a year the surrounding streets held more stalls than the hall did, the city's numbered plan inside was ignored from the first week, the seniority order never re-formed indoors, and not one dispute reached the municipal courts.
